items.key: ai:why are financial jobs disappearing? inside adp's latest employment report
items.text: Why Are Financial Jobs Disappearing? Inside ADP’s Latest Employment Report
items.article: According to the latest ADP National Employment Report, private employers added 90,000 jobs in September. America's labor market continued adding jobs in September, but the gains were concentrated in a handful of industries. Meanwhile, some of the nation's most prominent white-collar sectors continued to shrink. According to the latest ADP National Employment Report, private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, which was a rebound from weaker hiring in August. But beneath the headline number, two traditionally higher-paying office sectors moved in the opposite direction: Financial activities lost 16,000 jobs and professional and business services shed 11,000 positions. The new data has shown a growing divide in the labor market. While hiring remains healthy in areas like healthcare, education and hospitality, many office-based industries are grappling with slower demand and artificial intelligence taking over prior job functions Due to this, college graduates and young professionals are facing one of the most challenging white-collar job markets in years, experts say. “The easiest answer would be AI and the disappearance of entry level jobs in the financial sector, but it may be deeper than that,” Kevin Thompson, CEO of 9i Capital Group and host of the 9innings podcast, told Newsweek . “The real answer probably lies somewhere between AI and interest rates. With higher interest rates comes reduced financial activity.”

items.key: ai:met office issues october snow verdict as temperatures to drop across uk
items.text: Met Office issues October snow verdict as temperatures to drop across UK
items.article: The mercury hit 26.3C in Cambridge on Wednesday as most of the country experienced sunny conditions — but the unseasonal warmth won't last, Met Office forecasters say The Met Office has delivered its assessment on the likelihood of snow descending on the UK this October. Britain enjoyed a string of sweltering heatwaves throughout the summer, with temperatures frequently surpassing 35C and a number of records tumbling in the process. Temperatures have been steadily dropping over the past fortnight, with glorious sunshine giving way to heavier downpours and bitter, gusting winds. Despite this, Met Office forecasters have told said there are currently "no strong signals for widespread or disruptive snowfall across the UK during October". The meteorologists do, though, understand temperatures will drop in the coming days — to as low as 10C in the daytime. This is below the average for October and a plunge from the balmy weather the UK has experienced this week. A high of 26.3C was recorded in Cambridge on Wednesday. Holbeach in Lincolnshire saw the mercury reach 25.7C, while 24.9C was noted near Heathrow Airport in west London. But now brief cold snaps have not been entirely ruled out, with the higher reaches of Scotland considered the most probable locations to experience snow should wintry conditions take hold.

items.article: We've listened to nearly 1,500 podcasts from all around the U.S. and narrowed them down to 10 middle school and 10 high school finalists. What do Americans really know about their country? What do we mean when we think of "home"? When a father dies, what lessons does he leave for his son? And, was Andy Warhol a woman named Patricia? These topics – from fifth graders in Hewlett, N.Y., a high school student in Ann Arbor, Mich., an 11th grader in Cicero, Ill., and a middle schooler in Brooklyn – make up just a few of the many questions that students around the country turned into audio stories and sent us this year. Their answers to those questions are among our 2026 honorees as the best student podcasts in America. In its eighth year, the NPR Student Podcast Challenge received nearly 1,500 podcasts from students in 42 states and the District of Columbia. Our education team spent the summer listening to each of them, and from all those entries we've chosen the very best. So here are this year's finalists in our two main categories – grades five through eight and grades nine through 12. items.text: Here’s what AI leaders are saying about Trump’s new safety plan
items.article: The President says he has “the smartest people in the world watching over each other.” This is what they had to say about self-policing AI safety. Who needs legally binding regulations when you can be your own AI safety judge? After hosting a meal with Big Tech leaders on Tuesday, President Donald Trump responded to journalist questions about his artificial intelligence announcements in typical fashion. He said his previous claims regarding fears around AI safety being a “hoax” cooked up by Democrats no longer apply now that he’s renamed the technology to “ Super Intelligence .” He brushed off concerns that the government wasn’t enforcing enough AI guardrails because US companies are “dominating China.” And instead of ushering in federal AI regulations, Trump now has “the smartest people in the world watching over each other.” The people in question here are Google’s Sundar Pichai, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, XAI’s Elon Musk, and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. These tech leaders have signed the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities : a “morally binding” safety pledge that requires their companies to self-regulate their own AI technology with common sense guidelines and, seemingly, no ramifications for violating the agreement. All six of the signees provided press commentary at Trump’s behest, praising the self-policing plans as a positive step toward advancing AI technology, creating jobs, and dispersing negative public opinion
